certainty_reasoning: One documented passionate kiss - Wilde kissed Ives 'passionately' goodbye at the New Travellers' Club, the word being Cook's in the source quotation from the Ives diary - inside a close, teasing friendship that ran from the early 1890s to Wilde's last months (surviving letters to Ives from Oct. 1893 to Sept. 1900, plus prison messages via Sherard). No source read asserts sexual relations; the editorial note that Ives's anonymous A Book of Chains (1897) held 'poems bearing directly on his feelings for Wilde in prison' supports a romantic charge on Ives's side.
date_label: Met early 1890s (Cook: 'shortly after' Ives's July 1891 move to St James'; Lewis podcast: 'in about 1893'); kiss undated (New Travellers' Club period); friendship to Wilde's death, Nov. 1900.
summary: Ives met Wilde in early-1890s London and was drawn into his club and cafe circle; at the New Travellers' Club Wilde once kissed him 'passionately' goodbye (Ives's diary, via Cook). The friendship survived Wilde's imprisonment - Wilde sent word from Reading that he was 'greatly touched' by Ives's wish to visit, and Ives's anonymous 1897 A Book of Chains carried poems on his feelings for Wilde in prison - and continued through the Paris exile, where Wilde teased Ives's 'silly mania for secrecy' and called him 'a great baby', writing to him warmly until three months before his death.

sources.quote: It is a pleasure to me to see you. … I like to talk to you about literature, life, the progress of thought, its power to touch the world, its practical energy - subjects of no interest to others than ourselves.
sources.context: Wilde to Ives, 12 February [Postmark 1900], Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris - the same letter as the 'silly mania for secrecy' passage below, five paragraphs further on, where Wilde answers Ives's request that they meet somewhere out of sight
sources.supports: Wilde in his own hand, writing to Ives, saying plainly what the friendship was: a pleasure, and a private subject-matter shared by the two of them and nobody else. Wilde is refusing Ives's insistence on hidden meeting-places, so the sentence doubles as his statement that this bond needs no concealment - the sharpest first-hand characterization of the Ives-Wilde relationship in the record, and unmediated, unlike the diary-quoting passages below.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1218 (printed folio 1172 confirmed on the rendered page). Three intervening sentences elided with a spaced ellipsis; both sentences are from the same letter's closing two paragraphs.

sources.quote: …he enjoyed the company of Wilde and his circle in some of the new continental cafés and at the Authors' Club, the Lyric Club and the New Travellers' Club, where Wilde once kissed him 'passionately' goodbye.
sources.context: Cook, on Ives's expanding social circuit after meeting Wilde; 'passionately' is Cook quoting the Ives diary
sources.supports: The documented kiss: Wilde kissed Ives 'passionately' goodbye at the New Travellers' Club (undated by Cook)
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 161, printed folio 145 confirmed on rendered page. Leading clause of the sentence ('London, he said in October 1891, was a "grand place", and') elided; full sentence transcribed in dossier.

sources.quote: Please remember me very kindly to George Ives. I was greatly touched at hearing of his desire to come and see me. In the terrible solitude and silence in which one lives a message or a memory means a great deal. I hope he is hard at work writing books. I am very glad you know him. He is such a good fellow and so clever.
sources.context: Wilde to R. H. Sherard, from HM Prison, Reading, Wednesday [26 August 1896]
sources.supports: The bond held through prison: Ives sought to visit; Wilde 'greatly touched'
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 713, printed folio 662 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: Ives published A Book of Chains anonymously in 1897, which contained poems bearing directly on his feelings for Wilde in prison.
sources.context: Holland & Hart-Davis, editorial note on Wilde's mention of Ives in the letter to Sherard
sources.supports: Ives's side of the attachment: published poems on his feelings for Wilde (editorial characterization)
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 713, printed folio 662 confirmed on rendered page.

sources.quote: Don't have with me the silly mania for secrecy that makes you miss the value of things: to you it is of more importance to conceal your address from a friend, than to see your friend. … On the whole, George, you are a great baby. One can't help being angry with you.
sources.context: Wilde to Ives, 12 February [Postmark 1900], Hôtel d'Alsace, Paris; 'me' italicized in the original
sources.supports: Late-friendship intimacy and friction; the 'silly mania for secrecy' line is from this letter
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1218, printed folio 1172 confirmed on rendered page. Intervening paragraphs elided with spaced ellipsis; fuller text in dossier.

sources.quote: Yes: I have no doubt we shall win, but the road is long, and red with monstrous martyrdoms. Nothing but the repeal of the Criminal Law Amendment Act would do any good.
sources.context: Wilde to Ives, [Postmark 21 March 1898], Hôtel de Nice, Paris - written three years after the Act had convicted him, answering a letter of Ives's that does not survive here
sources.supports: Wilde's own naming of what he and Ives held in common: the campaign against the law that criminalized them. The first-person plural is the point - 'we shall win' puts Wilde inside Ives's cause, and the specific target he names is Ives's own, the repeal of the Criminal Law Amendment Act 1885. This is the passage most often cited as evidence that the friendship was political as well as personal, and it was missing from this record.
sources.provenance: Repo PDF page 1090 (printed folio 1044 confirmed on the rendered page).
